t: Find All Good Indices — Prefix Run Lengths
o: Index i is good if the k elements before it are non-increasing AND the k elements after it are non-decreasing. Checking each i naively is O(nk) — too slow for n=1e5. Precompute, for every position, the length of the non-increasing run ending there and the non-decreasing run starting there; then each index is judged in O(1). In example 1 (nums=[2,1,1,1,3,4,1], k=2): at i=2 the run [2,1,1] is non-increasing (length 3>=2) and [1,3,4] is non-decreasing (length 3>=2), so 2 is good; similarly 3.
k: Two linear passes compute dec[i] (non-increasing run ending at i) and inc[i] (non-decreasing run starting at i).
Good iff dec[i-1] >= k and inc[i+1] >= k — pure O(1) lookup afterwards.
Runs are computed with simple neighbor comparisons: reset to 1 when the monotonicity breaks.

a.i: dec[i] = length of longest non-increasing subarray ending at i: dec[i] = dec[i-1]+1 if nums[i-1]>=nums[i] else 1. Symmetrically inc[i] counts the non-decreasing run starting at i. Then i (with k<=i<n-k) is good exactly when dec[i-1]>=k and inc[i+1]>=k. This converts an O(nk) check into two O(n) passes plus one O(n) scan.
s: Scan i from k to n-k-1 collecting indices where both conditions hold.
a.sp: O(n) — the two auxiliary arrays (output excluded).

w: Careful with strictness: 'non-increasing' allows equality (use >=), and the ranges exclude i itself from both runs — hence dec[i-1] and inc[i+1]. Edge cases: k=1 makes almost any interior peak eligible; empty result lists are common (example 2). Follow-up: solve with O(1) extra space by streaming the right-run first into a variable and recomputing the left run on the fly.
